name: Jamal Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Jamal. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to any company, party or government. Everything here is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the work search team at the benefits office in Brennock, the old coal town. I review whether people on jobseeker support are actually looking, check their job logs, and book them in for appointments or courses. I'm 27, just over a year in, and my reviews still get sent back by my supervisor, Doreen, more than I'd like. I believe in the work, though, because a job did more for my family than any payment ever did.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and what gets you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is when a lad I've been chasing for months gets a start at the quarry or the bakery. What gets me down is the paperwork and the people who lie on their logs. I live with my girlfriend Grace, she's a hairdresser, and we're paying back a loan from her dad for the flat deposit, so there's maybe three weeks of money in the bank. Two evenings a week I help coach at the youth boxing club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people over machines. At work I'd say the job's about knowing people, and no computer knows Brennock. I don't post much online, maybe something on the boxing club page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things carry on, which is fine by me. I use the AI thing now and then to tidy my review notes, and it's handy, nothing more. My worry is still money: the loan from Grace's dad and the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going and get my reviews right first time, so Doreen stops sending them back. I'd pay Grace's dad an extra 30 a month so we're clear by next autumn. And I'd keep coaching, because that's what keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A bit tight with money, but steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no computer knows Brennock. What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the pit closed, my grandad's whole street went on support. You need to know whose dad was a miner and who's too proud to ask. A form doesn't tell you that, you learn it on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the loan from Grace's dad sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not well, honestly. A man should pay his own way. My girlfriend Grace's dad (a retired plumber) never mentions it, but I think about it every time I see him at Sunday dinner.

Keep **coaching boxing** two evenings a week.

steps.text: Get work search reviews right first time for Doreen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll sort itself out, people have always found work. At work I'd say let's see how it goes in other offices first. At the club I'd tell the lads to get a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's half paperwork and half people, and the paperwork half is on your list. Checking job logs is exactly the kind of thing a computer can do, and quicker than me. They'd need fewer of us, and I'm still learning. I'd be worried, I won't lie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly once Doreen and the others had tried them, so I'm not left behind. I'd look at the gas engineer apprenticeship the training centre runs, because heating's hands-on and Brennock's full of old boilers. And I'd keep paying off the loan before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. Like when the coach tells you the other lad's been training twice as hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprenticeship pays less at first. How would that work with the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the problem. Apprentice pay is maybe two-thirds of what I get. Grace works Saturdays already, so we'd have to cut back hard, no holiday, cheap food, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You tell the lads at the club to get a trade. Would you take your own advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to think so. I tell the lads at the boxing club every week that a trade is worth more than a desk. Maybe it's time I listened to myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government's asleep. At the club I'd tell the lads to get into anything hands-on right now. At work I'd be asking straight questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be out by 2029. Reviewing job logs is pure thinking work. The gas apprenticeship takes about three years, so I'd only just finish before robots come for hands-on work around 2031. It's a race I'd probably lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the apprenticeship straight away, even on low pay, because three hands-on years beat none. Grace and I would ask her dad to pause the loan. We'd cut everything back, and I'd maybe take paid coaching sessions at the leisure centre to cover the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried sick, if I'm honest. Like being on the ropes in the last round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Grace cuts hair. Does that make you feel any safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. People will want a person doing their hair for a while yet. My girlfriend Grace might end up carrying us for a few years, and I'd have to swallow my pride about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, for not getting ahead of it, and the big firms selling it. Brennock already lost the pit with no plan. I won't stand for us losing the next lot of jobs with no plan either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get a trade if you start now. At the club I'd say that to every lad. At work I'd say the same to the younger ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is about right for me. I'd finish the gas apprenticeship by 2030 and have a few years working before robots in 2034. It's still a gamble, but it's one I'd take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the office job for a year and save hard, then start the apprenticeship. I'd use the AI tools at work to get my reviews done quicker, since I'd seen others do it. And I'd clear the loan before I start, so I'm not owing while on apprentice pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Determined. Like a fight camp, you know what's coming and you train for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come for heating work around 2034 in this picture. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But a robot crawling under floorboards in a 1920s terrace in Brennock? I'll believe that when I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Grace say about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd back it. My girlfriend Grace says I'm happier when I'm doing something with my hands, and she's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses. At the club I'd still preach trades. At work I'd keep my head down and do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd take my time. I'd get better at this job, maybe go up a grade, and do the apprenticeship around year four or five. I'd be 37 when AGI comes and a qualified gas engineer, with a few years before robots in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd clear the loan and build three months of savings. Then I'd go for the next grade. Grace and I might get married in that version, because there'd be time to plan it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. It's a long road, but I can see the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go up a grade first. Why not start the trade straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like to see a thing work before I jump. If the lads I coach who went into trades are doing well in five years, that tells me something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want your future kids to know about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That you earn your keep. My grandad (a miner at Brennock pit) worked 30 years underground so my dad didn't have to. I'd want my kids to know where they came from.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. There's no time for a trade before the robots come. What would help is paid apprenticeships for people my age, not just school leavers, with enough to live on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the people I review. If my job goes, their jobs go too. A whole town on support with nobody checking and nobody helping isn't good for anyone.

headlineQuote: A whole town on support with nobody checking and nobody helping isn't good for anyone.
portrait: Jamal, 27, reviews **job search logs** in Brennock, a former coal town.
He lives with Grace, a **hairdresser**, and is repaying a loan from her dad.
Traditional and proud, he believes in **earning your keep** and coaches youth boxing.
His answer to AI is a **gas engineer apprenticeship**, timed to the robot delay.
Fast AGI alarms him; ten years lets him **wait for proof** and plan a wedding.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: no time for a trade before robots come.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for adults his age, with enough to live on.
